turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised a skeptical eyebrow, her gaze fixed upon the number 149. She inquired, with a distinct lack of warmth, whether this residence possessed a suitable hallway for receiving visitors, and, more importantly, a sufficient number of servants to maintain a proper appearance.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack stammered slightly, attempting to maintain a confident posture, and assured Lady Bracknell that the hallway was, of course, perfectly adequate and staffed by a most respectable number of servants – a sufficient complement, he believed, to meet any standard. He added, with a touch of hopeful eagerness, that they were, in fact, quite renowned for their discretion.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Jack’s assurances with an expression of profound doubt. She inquired, with a crispness that suggested he ought to be grateful for her attention, whether these servants possessed the necessary training in the art of silent observation and discreet removal of unpleasant callers. It is, after all, a skill of paramount importance in maintaining a certain level of decorum.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, eager to placate the formidable Lady Bracknell, hastened to explain that his servants were, without exception, trained in the utmost discretion, possessing a remarkable aptitude for both observation and, he added with a slightly strained smile, the subtle redirection of unwanted visitors. He truly believed they were quite exceptional in their ability to maintain a… a pleasing atmosphere, and he was certain they would meet with her complete approval. He hoped, at least.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell fixed Jack with a withering stare, her lips curving into a faint, almost cruel smile. She inquired if these servants, so remarkably adept at 'subtle redirection,' were, perhaps, also conversant in the proper handling of unwelcome correspondence and the judicious disposal of… *unsuitable* callers. It is, after all, a matter of considerable importance.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack flushed slightly, his eagerness momentarily overshadowed by a rising sense of panic. He assured Lady Bracknell that his household staff were meticulously trained in all matters of correspondence and, with a nervous chuckle, volunteered that any… *unsuitable* visitors were handled with the utmost efficiency and, he hoped, with a degree of tact that would be entirely to her satisfaction.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow, her gaze unwavering. She inquired of Mr. Worthing, with an almost clinical detachment, whether his household possessed a comprehensive understanding of the proper protocols for dealing with *family* correspondence – a matter, she suggested, that could prove surprisingly delicate, particularly when dealing with… sensitive matters. It would be most regrettable, wouldn't it, if certain indiscretions were to reach the wrong ears?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack stammered slightly, attempting a reassuring smile, and explained that his butler, Jenkins, oversaw all family correspondence with the utmost care and discretion. He added that Jenkins was, in fact, rather particular about the quality of the paper used, believing it reflected greatly on the sender’s judgment – a detail, Jack hoped, that demonstrated a commitment to propriety.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s mention of Jenkins and his fastidious paper preferences with a degree of skepticism that bordered on amusement. She inquired, with a pointedness that made Jack visibly wince, whether this Jenkins possessed any demonstrable experience in the *suppression* of inconvenient truths, a skill, she pronounced, far more valuable than a mere appreciation for stationery.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack swallowed, his Adam's apple bobbing nervously as he attempted to formulate a reply. He assured Lady Bracknell that Jenkins, while perhaps not formally trained in… *suppression*, possessed a remarkable aptitude for discretion and a profound understanding of the importance of maintaining appearances, qualities, he believed, that often proved more effective than any explicit instruction. He hoped, with a desperate smile, that this would be satisfactory.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell tapped a long, lacquered fingernail against her cheek, her expression unreadable for a moment. She then inquired of Mr. Worthing, in a tone that suggested she found the entire discussion rather diverting, whether this 'remarkable aptitude for discretion' extended to matters beyond the selection of stationery and the management of household staff – specifically, she asked, did Mr. Jenkins possess any understanding of the proper handling of… *scandals*?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling the pressure acutely, attempted a light chuckle, hoping to diffuse the increasingly tense atmosphere. He explained that while Jenkins hadn't, to his knowledge, encountered any *actual* scandals, his inherent discretion certainly prevented any potential for their emergence, a preventative measure, Jack suggested, which was arguably even more valuable. He offered Lady Bracknell a slightly strained smile, desperately hoping she would find this sufficiently reassuring.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow, a gesture that conveyed more disdain than any spoken word. She inquired of Mr. Worthing, with an almost clinical detachment, whether he considered this ‘preventative measure’ to be a substitute for genuine moral rectitude, or merely a convenient evasion of unpleasantness.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack stammered slightly, attempting to regain some semblance of composure. He insisted that, of course, moral rectitude was paramount, and that his, and by extension Jenkins', actions were always guided by a sincere desire to uphold the highest standards of propriety. He added, with a touch of desperation, that a commitment to discretion was simply a practical application of those very principles.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing with an expression of profound skepticism, her lips curving into a faint, almost pitying smile. She inquired whether this supposed ‘commitment to discretion’ was, in fact, a carefully constructed facade, designed to conceal a lamentable lack of genuine principle. It seemed, she observed, that Mr. Jenkins’s talents, and indeed Mr. Worthing’s own, were being employed in a rather ingenious exercise in obfuscation.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen declared, with an air of wounded innocence, that surely such a thorough grilling was unnecessary, as her intentions regarding Mr. Worthing were perfectly clear. It was, she insisted, rather tiresome to have one’s affections subjected to such… scrutiny. She glanced pointedly at her mother, clearly implying that the entire situation was a reflection of Lady Bracknell's overbearing nature.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell observed Miss Fairfax with a glacial composure, then turned her attention back to Mr. Worthing, her voice dripping with a delicate irony. She remarked that while the young lady's sentiments, however passionately expressed, were hardly a substitute for a demonstrable pedigree, it appeared Mr. Worthing was attempting to navigate a particularly treacherous landscape of social convention. It seemed, she suggested, that a more detailed exploration of his background was now not merely advisable, but absolutely essential.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack attempted a reassuring smile, though it felt strained even to his own perception. He assured Lady Bracknell that he understood the importance of a thorough examination and would, of course, provide any information she deemed necessary to clarify his position and, he hoped, alleviate her concerns. He added, with a slight tremor in his voice, that he was at her disposal.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing with a look that suggested he was attempting to navigate a particularly complicated maze with a blindfold. She inquired, with a tone of academic detachment, whether he possessed any discernible connection to the landed gentry, and if so, precisely what form that connection might take. It appeared, she observed, that an individual of his… apparent resources, required a more rigorous investigation than a mere recitation of platitudes could provide.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling a flush creep up his neck, stammered that his family history was, admittedly, somewhat… unconventional, and that he would be delighted to elaborate, if Lady Bracknell would permit him. He hoped, he added with a nervous smile, that she wouldn’t find his circumstances unduly distressing.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen informed Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell remarked that Gwendolen was not engaged to anyone and explained that an engagement should come as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, and that she or Gwendolen’s father would inform her of the fact. She added that it was hardly a matter for her to arrange for herself and then announced that she had a few questions to put to Mr. Worthing, instructing Gwendolen to wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen protested to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell instructed Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell repeated her instruction for Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen acknowledged Lady Bracknell’s instruction.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell invited Jack to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack thanked Lady Bracknell but stated that he preferred standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell explained that she felt bound to tell Jack that he was not listed among the eligible young men, though she shared the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. She added that she was ready to enter his name if his answers were what a mother required and then inquired whether he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack admitted that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that a man should always have an occupation and that there were too many idle men in London. She then asked him how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack replied that he was twenty-nine years old.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell commented that it was a very good age to be married and stated that she believed a man who desired to get married should know either everything or nothing, asking him which he knew.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack responded that he knew nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that she did not approve of anything that tampered with natural ignorance and that ignorance was like a delicate exotic fruit. She continued by criticizing modern education and suggesting that it would be dangerous to the upper classes. Finally, she asked about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stated that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired whether the income was in land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack clarified that it was chiefly in investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell observed that land had ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure and that it only provided position. She then asked about a country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack explained that he had a country house with fifteen hundred acres attached, but that he did not depend on it for his income, adding that the poachers seemed to be the only ones benefiting from it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired about the number of bedrooms in the country house and then asked if he had a town house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stated that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham, adding that he could get it back at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed that she did not know Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack explained that Lady Bloxham did not go about very much and that she was considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell remarked that age was no guarantee of respectability of character and asked for the number of the house in Belgrave Square.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack replied that the number was 149.
